hints: Look past the CO2H group they all share and focus on what is different, an alkyl group, a secondary alcohol, and a ketone.
Notice that NaHCO3 will fizz with every carboxylic acid, so it cannot tell these three apart, while warm acidified dichromate turns green only with the alcohol.
Consider which carbonyl test responds to ketones as well as aldehydes, and use it to pick out the keto-acid and leave the simple acid by elimination.
walkthrough:
**Name the functional groups in each liquid**

Lovely start, let's label what we have. Think of them as family members with one thing in common.

$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ = propanoic acid, carboxylic acid only

$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H}$ = 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, carboxylic acid + secondary alcohol

$\text{CH}_3\text{COCO}_2\text{H}$ = 2-oxopropanoic acid, carboxylic acid + ketone

**See why test 1 must be warm acidified dichromate**

All three contain $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, so all three fizz with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to give $\text{CO}_2$. That test gives no separation.

Warm acidified dichromate is an oxidising agent and only oxidises the secondary alcohol:
$$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} (\text{orange}) \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+} (\text{green})$$
Only $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H}$ turns orange to green. The simple acid and the keto-acid stay orange.

**See why test 2 must be 2,4-DNPH reagent**

Now we need to separate the remaining two. 2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone $\text{C=O}$.

Only $\text{CH}_3\text{COCO}_2\text{H}$ contains a ketone, so only it gives the orange precipitate. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ gives no reaction.

**Put the identification together**

Positive with dichromate only means the hydroxy-acid. Positive with 2,4-DNPH only means the keto-acid. Negative with both means propanoic acid.

That pair of results uniquely identifies all three liquids.

options.A: Incorrect. NaHCO3 gives effervescence with all three carboxylic acids, so test 1 does not separate them. Although 2,4-DNPH correctly picks out the keto-acid, the hydroxy-acid and propanoic acid would both be negative and remain confused.
options.B: Incorrect. NaHCO3 again reacts with all three, so it is useless here. Tollens' reagent is also useless because it only gives a silver mirror with aldehydes, and none of these is an aldehyde (the carbonyl present is a ketone), so all three would be negative.
options.C: Correct. Warm acidified dichromate oxidises only the secondary alcohol in CH3CH(OH)CO2H, turning orange to green. 2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate only with the ketone in CH3COCO2H. CH3CH2CO2H is negative in both tests, so each liquid has a unique pair of results.
options.D: Incorrect. Warm acidified dichromate correctly identifies the hydroxy-acid, but Tollens' reagent fails as test 2. Tollens' oxidises aldehydes only, not ketones, so the keto-acid CH3COCO2H gives no silver mirror and cannot be distinguished from propanoic acid.
